query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermomechanical treatments that increase defect density and promote local chemical ordering can stabilize a dual-phase microstructure in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by enabling controlled nucleation and distribution of ordered intermetallic (BCC/B2) precipitates within an FCC matrix. This microstructure balances high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or conventionally annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs with a mixed phase composition (primarily FCC with some disordered BCC/B2 regions) and relatively low defect density.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment regime, for example, cold deformation (e.g., rolling) followed by a specific annealing protocol (e.g., heating to ~900 °C for a fixed time and then quenching) designed to significantly increase dislocation density and drive local chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Maintain precise control of strain (deformation amount), annealing temperature, and time such that defect density is enhanced without causing excessive coarsening of precipitates; compare treated samples against untreated or conventionally heat-treated controls.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced defect density (dislocations, grain boundary sites) and local chemical ordering that act as nucleation sites for fine, coherent ordered BCC/B2 precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Increased defects accelerate the nucleation of ordered phases within the FCC matrix. The resultant fine-scale, well-distributed precipitates help stabilize the microstructure by impeding further undesirable phase transformations and accommodating multiple deformation mechanisms, thereby preserving high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and maintaining toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermomechanically treated samples will exhibit an increased fraction of finely dispersed, ordered BCC/B2 precipitates in a predominantly FCC matrix relative to the untreated baseline. This altered phase stability is expected to correlate with enhanced high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance while retaining good environmental resistance and cryogenic toughness.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs processed without the tailored thermomechanical treatment, which exhibit lower defect densities and less controlled local ordering, resulting in a less optimal balance of phases.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is confined to processing conditions that avoid over-aging or precipitate coarsening. Its validity may depend on maintaining precise treatment temperatures, strain levels, and cooling rates; extreme treatments may lead to excessive phase aggregation or unintended brittle intermetallic formation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between defect density, local chemical ordering, and the exact phase fractions remains uncertain, as does the scale of improvement in mechanical and irradiation properties. Further optimization of the processing parameters is required to generalize the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one set subjected to the tailored thermomechanical treatment (e.g., cold rolling followed by annealing at ~900 °C and quenching) and one set processed via conventional heat treatment (minimal deformation prior to annealing). Characterize the phase fractions using XRD, EBSD, and TEM, and measure mechanical properties (high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance proxy through irradiation experiments, and cryogenic toughness testing).
measurements: Phase fraction and distribution (FCC vs. BCC/B2) from EBSD and TEM
Defect density quantification (dislocation density from TEM)
Mechanical property tests (tensile tests at high and cryogenic temperatures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored thermomechanical treatment does not lead to a statistically significant increase in defect density and a corresponding controlled increase in the fine ordered BCC/B2 precipitates (as compared to the control) and does not yield improved mechanical and irradiation properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

EBSD phase and IPF maps were obtained from the central gage regions of specimens, as shown in Fig. 9(a–d). The 10Co and 20Co alloys show a transition of deformation mechanism from dislocation slip to deformation twinning as the temperature decreases from room temperature to cryogenic temperature (Figs 7(a,b) and 9(a,b)). Thus, the strain hardening rate decreases more slowly at cryogenic temperature than at room temperature (Fig. 4(c,d)). In the 30Co and 35Co alloys, most of fcc phases are transformed to bcc phases after the cryogenic-temperature tensile test (Fig. 3(c)), but the 35Co alloy shows the higher fraction of bcc phase (86%) than the 30Co alloy (47%) at the true strain of 0.34 (Fig. 9(c,d)). This indicates the higher transformation rate in the 35Co alloy than that in the 30Co alloy. The XRD spectra of the as-cast and both processed samples is shown in Figure 3. The as-cast sample shows BCC/B2 phases whereas both processed samples show FCC phase along with BCC/B2 phases. The evolution of the FCC phase is likely due to BCC/B2 phase transformation into FCC during high strain-rate processing. In HEAs, BCC/B2 to FCC phase transformations have been shown in earlier studies as well. The peak intensity of the FCC phase is higher in the SFP_1800 sample as compared to SFP_400 sample, which indicates a higher fraction of phase transformation in SFP_1800. Further, EBSD phase maps (Figure S2) were extracted in order to quantify the phase fraction. The FCC phase transformation obtained in the SFP_400 sample is 38%, while that for SFP_1800 is 55%. The likely reason for the phase transformation is the significant increase in the defect density, namely, dislocation density, point defects, and GB fraction, which increases the system energy during SFP. Other than B2/BCC and FCC phases, an AlNi-rich phase is also observed with a weak peak intensity in the SFP_400 sample. The phase transformations of the Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 HEA have been studied in this research paper. The alloy underwent hot forging, cold rolling, annealing at and quenching from 1323 K, and isothermal holding, at 873 K. The as-quenched HEA is a single FCC. After the 873-K isothermal holding, the coherent fine L12 particles precipitated homogeneously in the FCC matrix. In addition, cellular precipitation occurred, resulting in the transformation of the high-temperature FCC phase into lamellae of the low-temperature FCC phase and L12 phase. The colonies nucleated and grew from the grain boundaries. The grain boundary moved with the growing tips of the newly formed lamellar FCC and L12 phases, and the lamellar FCC grains had the same orientation as that of one neighboring FCC grain and grew into the other neighboring FCC grain, with a different orientation. The lamellar L12 grains had the following composition: Ni60Co8Cr6Fe6Al20, and the FCC grains had the following composition: Ni31Co15Cr28Fe21Al4. The lamellar L12 phase was rich in Ni and Al, and lean in Co, Cr, and Fe, and the lamellar FCC phase was contrary to this.

reading.lever: Use tailored thermomechanical treatments to modulate defect density and local chemical ordering in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
reading.why: Because prior studies show that controlled deformation and thermal treatments can direct phase transformations via defect engineering, a strategy not yet applied to this alloy system for simultaneously optimizing high-temperature, irradiation, environmental, and cryogenic properties.
